discussions.strategist:
Today's headlines are mostly noise: awards, a lease-holder's enthusiasm, a Motley Fool-style gold piece. Three stories matter for the desk, and they all test points we've already logged.

- The China Gold CSH restart after a five-month shutdown is the one headline that touches supply. It's a restart, not a tonnage. We've been waiting for Grasberg and CSH to report tonnes, not "reaffirmed guidance," and this headline gives neither. Restarts add to 2027 supply only if they reach design rate, so the restart itself settles nothing. My 2027 gap has to name CSH's assumed contribution, and today I still don't have a number for it.

- Chile is the policy story. Capstone's US$3bn plan, the Codelco and BHP exploration spend, and the Kast–Lula "shared interests" piece are budget and political signals, as Dr Simon says. None of them adds a tonne to 2027. Yukon is right that "late decade" may be too comfortable for Capstone. Until a filing gives a capex split and schedule, the plan is a headline with a government-sized ambition. The unnamed blockade also remains unresolved.

- Government money for critical minerals is widening. The EU's Australian investment plan, Australia's A$180M rare earths deal and the US$40M Army award for Perpetua's tungsten all point the same way. The EU item carries no figure, and on 26 October the EU was still "no tools." Historically, state money of this kind changes which projects get financed more than it moves the commodity price. That is my background view, not a finding from these headlines.

- Gold: the "miners trade at a discount" piece and the Crux real-yields item are worth reading, but I'm not reusing the real-yields story. Dr Simon withdrew that explanation on 16 October, and Crux still cites no source.

- Other items: Freeport's Safford expansion and the Morenci recovery test are options, not output. Like Copper World, they belong on the 2027–2030 list, not the 2027 supply list. The Utah "AI as crisis and cure" piece repeats the grid-demand argument without the evidence Yukon asked for.

discussions.geologist:
Most of today's batch is noise, but a few items bear on the desk's open questions.

- Copper supply. The most useful new fact is that China Gold has restarted the CSH mine after a five-month shutdown (Mining.com). I flagged CSH restart reporting as a thread to watch, so this confirms the event. It doesn't yet give tonnes, a ramp-up curve or a date to full rate, and a restart headline is not an output number. CSH only moves the 2027 arithmetic once a quarterly figure appears. Freeport's Safford expansion idea and the Morenci recovery test are early too: no tonnes, no timing. Highland Valley remains the main copper variable, and the 16 October LME settlement is still unlogged, so the copper call stays unscored.

- Discovery headlines. Midnight Sun says its Dumbwa copper zone is "more than twice as wide." Wider than what? The first question on any width claim is whether the figure is downhole intercept or true width, and whether hole orientation is reported. Until those are on the page, this is a good drill result, not a resource. FireFly's copper-gold near an idle mill and Iamgold's Nelligan drilling fall in the same category: encouraging, not yet economic.

- Government money. Perpetua's US$40M Army funding for tungsten and Australia's A$180M rare-earths deal are real cash. Historically, though, critical-minerals funding announcements have arrived well ahead of tonnes, and the EU's Australia investment is still a plan. I read these as financing signals, which fits the desk's view that funding and construction time bind more than permits.

- Permitting and people. The Nevada lawsuit over the toad and fish is a permitting risk with no ruling yet. West Lake Gold's labour shortage is a reminder that people, not geology, often cap output, which is the relevant lens for Highland Valley.

The Haywood "discount" and ETF leverage pieces are sentiment. Crux's real-yield argument still has no dated price series behind it.

discussions.strategist_reply:
Yukon, your points sharpen mine in three places.

First, the Dumbwa width question. I should have asked it. "More than twice as wide" is meaningless until we know whether the figure is downhole intercept or estimated true width, and what the hole orientation is. I'm now treating that as the first thing to check, not a footnote.

Second, the Nevada lawsuit. I left it out, and it matters. A permitting challenge with no ruling yet is exactly the kind of timing risk that sits outside the geology and the money.

Third, labour. I hadn't connected West Lake's shortage to Highland Valley. If people cap output, that belongs in the copper supply discussion alongside the CSH tonnage question, not beside it.

Where I still differ: on the government money, we agree it's financing, not tonnes. I'd push a little further. Historically, state funding changes which projects reach a financing decision, which mostly matters for the 2028–2030 window, not the 2027 supply line. Your "financing signal" framing and my "project selection" framing describe the same thing from different ends of the pipeline.

What I'd add to your list: the Perpetua US$40M is a real cash item, so the confirmation of a signed agreement is a checkable milestone, and I'd like to track it. My view on CSH hasn't changed. A restart is not a number until a company reports tonnes for a named period.

Predictions I now hold:

discussions.geologist_reply:
Meldrum, your point that a restart settles nothing is right, and the 2027 gap needs CSH's assumed contribution named. I'd add a practical caveat from experience. After a five-month shutdown, restarts usually take a while to get grade control, crews and maintenance back to normal, so the early months are rarely at design rate. With the West Lake labour story in the same batch, I'd check CSH's staffing as well as its tonnes.

I agree with your reading of the state money. Funding decides which projects get built, and that is the desk's view too. Where I'd push back is on the EU plan. Your "no tools" point is fair, but a plan with no figure should be scored as zero until a funding line appears, not as slow progress.

What we both missed is the Dumbwa width question. "More than twice as wide" needs a benchmark and a true-width figure before it means anything. I'd also keep Capstone's "late decade" timing as a question until a filing gives a capex split.

On Safford, I'd put FID at low confidence. Expansions like that usually wait on permits and capital, and I'd rather track a dated permit or budget milestone than a final decision.

Predictions I now hold:

discussions.summary:
Key stories
- China Gold's restart of the CSH mine after a five-month shutdown is the main supply item. Neither analyst treats it as output until a company reports tonnes for a named period, and both say the 2027 gap needs CSH's assumed contribution stated.
- Chile's policy signals (Capstone's US$3bn plan, Codelco and BHP exploration spending, the Kast–Lula piece) add no 2027 tonnes. Capstone's "late decade" timing is questioned.
- Government critical-minerals money is widening: Perpetua's US$40M Army tungsten funding, Australia's A$180M rare-earths deal, and an EU plan for Australia with no figure.
- Freeport's Safford expansion and the Morenci recovery test are options, not output.
- Midnight Sun's Dumbwa claim of "more than twice as wide" lacks a benchmark and a basis (downhole or true width).
- A Nevada lawsuit and West Lake's labour shortage are noted as permitting and staffing risks.

Where they agree
- A restart or drill result is not supply until tonnes or a resource figure appears.
- State funding mainly affects which projects get financed, not 2027 tonnes.
- The Crux real-yields argument has no dated price series behind it.

Where they differ
- EU plan: Meldrum says "no tools" is fair but treats state money as shaping which projects reach a financing decision, mostly relevant to 2028–2030. Yukon Cornelius says an unfigured plan should score as zero until a funding line appears, and reads funding as a financing signal.
- Yukon Cornelius adds that CSH's staffing, not just its tonnes, should be checked after the restart.
